title: The city in thirds: outcomes by who lives in the neighborhood
question: If neighborhoods are sorted into thirds by income, by race and ethnicity, by birthplace, by renting and by age, do like applications end differently?
finding: In the lowest-income third of neighborhoods 28.0% of 1,660 not approved against 25.8% expected; in the highest-income third 24.0% of 2,077 not approved against 26.0% expected. In the third with the fewest white residents 30.9% of 1,315 not approved against 26.9% expected; in the third with the most, 27.1% of 1,497 not approved against 29.2% expected. Outright refusals run the other way (1.8% against 2.9%), so the gap is made of withdrawals and cancellations. Applications that mention an enforcement notice fail more often (38.7% of 326 against 26.1% of the rest) and are 6.2% of cases in the fewest-white third against 7.0% in the most-white third; allowing for that, the fewest-white third’s gap is +4.2% and still beyond chance (South of Market: 24 of the 52 more than expected). 2 of 24 groups sit further from their expected rate than chance would explain: lowest third by the share of white residents (+4.0% on 1,315); highest third by the share of Asian residents (+2.6% on 1,848). Neighbors ask for a review 71 times per 1,000 residential permits in the third with the most white residents and 20 in the third with the fewest; by income, 74 in the highest third and 21 in the lowest.
how: Neighborhoods are ranked on each Census measure (2020-24 survey) and cut into three groups of equal number; every decided application since 2015 is pooled within its group. “Expected” applies the citywide rate for the same approval type, kind of proposal and period to each case, so it shows what the group’s own mix of cases would produce anywhere in the city. “Filed after an enforcement notice” = the application’s text mentions a notice of violation, an enforcement case or unpermitted work; the second gap also holds that equal. “Beyond chance” is judged at about the 1-in-100 level; with 24 groups compared, about one table in four would show one such group by luck alone. Review requests are neighbors’ discretionary-review filings per 1,000 full building permits on homes and apartment buildings.
limits: A difference between places is not proof of bias. Places differ in what is proposed, in zoning, lot sizes, building ages and land prices, and in who chooses to apply at all; applicants also withdraw for their own reasons (money, a sale, a redesign filed under a new number). The thirds describe areas, not applicants: nothing is known or assumed about who filed any application, and a lower-income neighborhood’s applicants include developers and absentee owners. The measures overlap heavily (the highest-income third and the whitest third are largely the same neighborhoods), so the rows are eight views of one pattern, not eight findings. Most non-approvals are withdrawals, which the applicant chooses; applications forced by a code-enforcement notice are abandoned more often and are more common in some areas. The hearing minutes, roll-call votes and appeal decisions now being collected would show who voted, who objected and what reason was recorded in each case.
